answer:
Let me take the objection seriously, because the "developing Christology" argument is a real historical claim, not just a rhetorical move. But I'd push back on the premise that Mark and Matthew present a "modest" Jesus.

Notice what's actually in the earlier material even by the objector's own framing: the Son of Man title itself is drawn from Daniel 7, where that figure is enthroned alongside the Ancient of Days and given everlasting dominion and worship by all peoples — this is not a humble human self-designation, it's an apocalyptic claim to share divine glory. So even the "modest" title is doing enormous theological work. The material I have doesn't let me adjudicate verse-by-verse what's unique to John versus the Synoptics in fine detail, and I won't pretend otherwise — that's a fair limit to name.

But here's the deeper problem with "legend develops upward over time" as applied here: the earliest datable Christian confession we have, embedded in Philippians 2:5–11 (widely regarded as pre-Pauline hymnic material, therefore earlier than any Gospel, canonical or otherwise), already says Christ existed in the form of God and applies to Him the Isaiah 45 language of every knee bowing to YHWH alone. That is the highest possible Christology, attested extremely early — decades before John, and arguably contemporaneous with or prior to Mark. The trajectory the objection assumes (low Christology early, high Christology late) doesn't actually fit: high Christology is there at the earliest layer we can access. John's "I AM" sayings and the Word made flesh are an unpacking of what was already confessed, not an invention decades later.

The "I am" in John 8:58 doesn't stand alone either — it's the same pattern found across the whole New Testament corpus: Hebrews' Father addressing the Son as "O God" (Hebrews 1:8, quoting Psalm 45:6), 1 Timothy 3:16's confession of God manifested in flesh, and the repeated application of Isaiah's divine-only prerogatives to Jesus. These come from different authors, different communities, different genres — not a single late trajectory but multiple independent witnesses converging on the same identification. That's harder to explain as one community's escalating legend and easier to explain as diverse testimony to something the earliest church already believed: that in Jesus, the God of Israel had visited His people. The real question isn't "did divinity get invented late" but "which explanation accounts for the earliness and diversity of this belief" — and legendary development, on the evidence actually before us, doesn't fit near as well as the church's own answer: My Lord and my God.

transcript.content: Look, the plain fact is this: in Mark and Matthew—the earliest Gospel traditions we have—Jesus never utters the words "I am God" or claims outright divinity. He calls himself "Son of Man," he points to God as "Father," he speaks about the Kingdom coming. Only in John, written decades later and by an unknown author in a Hellenistic community far removed from Palestine, do we get the explicit "I am" statements that theologians read as deity claims. That's not how an eyewitness testimony develops—that's how legend does. The more time passes, the higher the Christology climbs. So either Jesus actually said these things and three Gospel writers somehow forgot to include them, or the latest writer is doing what late religious communities do: reading divinity back into an earlier, more modest Jewish teacher. Which seems more historically plausible to you?
